planting.note: Plant divisions of the small tuber-like rootstock in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade; tuberous comfrey spreads slowly from short rhizomes rather than a single deep taproot, so it is easier to contain than other comfreys.

directions: Tuberous comfrey is a lower-growing, non-aggressive European comfrey species that spreads slowly from a cluster of small tuber-like swollen roots rather than a single deep taproot, making it considerably easier to control than common or Russian comfrey. In late spring, nodding clusters of pale cream to pale yellow tubular flowers open above a loose rosette of bristly, elliptic leaves, a notably softer color than the blue-violet or purple-pink flowers typical of other cultivated comfreys. It tolerates woodland shade and part-shade conditions better than most comfrey species and is grown chiefly as an ornamental groundcover or botanical curiosity rather than for bulk mulch production, since its compact size yields far less leaf matter per clump. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or crown divisions in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; give prickly comfrey ample room, since established clumps are long-lived and difficult to remove.

directions: Prickly comfrey is a tall, robust comfrey species native to the Caucasus and parts of western Asia, covered in distinctly stiff, bristly hairs that are rougher to the touch than the softer hairs of common comfrey. Clusters of tubular flowers open pink to red-violet in bud and mature to vivid blue, creating an attractive two-tone effect on the same flowering stem. Along with common comfrey, prickly comfrey is one of the two parent species crossed to produce the vigorous hybrid Russian comfrey (Symphytum x uplandicum), widely grown as a dynamic accumulator for mulch and liquid fertilizer production. Plant it in fertile, moisture-retentive soil where its coarse, spreading habit has room, as established clumps are long-lived and difficult to remove once settled.

common_name: Bocking 4 Comfrey (Russian Comfrey Selection for Compost Activation)

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or crown divisions 3-4 inches deep in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Bocking 4 is sterile and must be propagated vegetatively, never from seed.

directions: Bocking 4 is one of several named Russian comfrey selections developed through mid-20th-century variety trials of Symphytum x uplandicum conducted by the Henry Doubleday Research Association (now Garden Organic) in Britain, alongside the better-known Bocking 14. Like Bocking 14, it is a sterile selection propagated only from root cuttings or crown divisions rather than seed, so plantings stay put rather than spreading as a garden weed. Bocking 4 is generally favored by gardeners for compost-heap activation rather than liquid feed production, since its leaves are reported to break down readily into a balanced, nutrient-rich addition that speeds decomposition of woody or carbon-heavy compost materials. As with other Russian comfrey selections, establish it in a permanent bed in fertile soil, since the deep roots make later relocation difficult.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in partial shade; grown for its variegated foliage rather than mulch production, so remove any solid-green reverted shoots promptly.

directions: Variegated Russian comfrey is an ornamental sport of Russian comfrey selected for broad, irregular cream to white margins on its coarse, bristly-hairy leaves, a striking contrast to the solid green foliage of the species. It is noticeably less vigorous and more compact than plain Russian comfrey or the Bocking strains grown for mulch production, making it better suited to a shaded border or woodland edge than a dedicated cutting bed. Clusters of tubular, pink-to-blue flowers open above the foliage in late spring, but the plant is grown primarily as a foliage specimen; shear off any shoots that revert to solid green promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will eventually overtake the variegated form. Divide in spring if clumps become congested, discarding any all-green sections to maintain strong variegation.

common_name: Hidcote Pink Comfrey (Pink-Flowered Dwarf Comfrey Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Hidcote Pink is a named selection of dwarf comfrey grown as a companion to the better-known 'Hidcote Blue', sharing the same low, mat-forming habit and broad, hairy, dark-green foliage but offering soft pink buds that open to pale pink tubular flowers instead of blue-violet. Like its sibling selection, it blooms on arching stems in early spring ahead of most other shade perennials, then persists as a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover through the rest of the season. It spreads at a manageable pace by rhizomes and light self-seeding, far less aggressively than common or Russian comfrey, and tolerates drier shade once established better than most comfrey species. Use it to extend the dwarf comfrey color range in a woodland or shade garden planted alongside hostas, ferns, and epimediums.
